title: Theo's Perfect Boat Problem
markdown:
The sky blazed pink and orange, a spectacular promise. Mabel the marmot wiggled her whiskers. A fizz of excitement. Today was the Sunny Meadow Boat Show, and her best friend Theo the fox would show his model boats.

"Breakfast, my little marmot!" Gran Ada called, warm as sunbeams through oak. Mabel danced down the tunnel, paws tapping packed earth. Toasted sunflower seeds, sweet berry jam. "Today will be brilliant!" Her fluffy tail jiggled. Gran Ada's eyes crinkled. "Theo's boats are always perfect little treasures."

They were. Theo spent ages in his den, whittling and painting, bushy tail flicking. Every plank glued just so, every sail rigged with impossible neatness. This year's prize was the Ducky Delight: polished wood, a tiny blue flag snapping in an imagined breeze. Theo declared it his finest work.

The meadow buzzed. Theo was already there, proud smile, tail thumping. "Mabel! Gran Ada! You've got to see!" The Ducky Delight sat on a velvet cushion, catching sun, a magnificent tiny vessel.

Then a peculiar thing: a family of fluffy ducklings waddled up, stately mother behind. Important quacks. The ducklings bobbed agreement. To Theo's utter surprise, the whole flock began to follow the model. They pecked its gleaming hull. Tiny webbed feet paddled in imaginary water.

"They think it's in charge," Theo whispered. Ears drooped. Confidence dimmed.

Mabel giggled — it was a bit funny, real ducks taking orders from a wooden captain — but Theo looked distressed. "My prize boat. The judges will be here. They can't see this chaos." More ducks arrived, equally convinced. Happy quacks, fluffy feathers, comical commotion.

"Oh, Theo. It's just too realistic. It looks like a commanding captain."

His shoulders slumped. "I worked so hard to make it perfect."

Gran Ada patted his paw. "Sometimes perfection has unexpected consequences. Perhaps we can think of a clever solution together."

Mabel's eyes sparkled. "I've got it. Your boat is too good for a captain. The ducks need a boat of their own — slightly less perfect. A decoy!"

"Less perfect? Why make a boat that isn't?"

"So they'll follow that one!" Words tumbling. "Friendly, not quite as important. Before the judges get here."

Theo's ears perked. A boat that wasn't perfect felt strange. He trusted Mabel. Determined flick of tail, spare wood, a pot of bright yellow paint. Mabel gathered fabric scraps and shiny leaves. Paws flew. Theo whittled a cheerful, slightly wobbly beak and a welcoming face. Mabel glued a wonderfully lopsided flower of fallen petals, sweet in the air. The new boat was warm and a little rough under Theo's paws — a charming contrast to the polished masterpiece. Delightfully imperfect.

Just as the lead judge, a stately badger with a very important clipboard, approached, Mabel set the new boat near the pond's edge. "Quack!" The mother spotted the bright arrival, pointed her beak, and the family paddled over with happy splashes, nudging the flowered vessel, content.

The judge peered at the Ducky Delight. Whiskers twitched. He circled slowly. "Remarkable. The attention to detail… astonishing. Craftsmanship unparalleled. A masterful recreation." A decisive note. A faint smile.

Theo's tail thumped. He beamed at Mabel. The Ducky Delight was saved for judging. The ducks had a friendlier admiral, which seemed, on the whole, better for ducks.

He did not declare the day amazing to the sky at large. He looked at the wobbly yellow decoy, already slightly damp from devoted beaks, and at his perfect boat, which had been too convincing for its own good.

"I wonder," he said, "whether next year's entry should have a slightly crooked flag on purpose — or whether I'll just pack two boats, and let the ducks vote."

Mabel, who had invented the opposition party, voted for two. Gran Ada packed jam sandwiches, which needed no varnish at all.
